posts.body:
You're outgrowing your brokerage if you're solving problems alone that should be solved with a team.

I see it all the time. An agent is closing deals, hitting their numbers, but they're doing it in isolation. Nobody's helping them think through the hard transactions. Nobody's backing them up when something breaks. They call their broker and get a voicemail. They're winning but they feel like they're losing because there's no one in the trenches with them. That's not sustainable. That's not a career. That's a grind that has an expiration date. The best agents don't leave because they're unhappy with money. They leave because they're tired of being alone while they're building something.

If you want to talk about what we're building at Lifestyle Design Realty, send me a DM.

Had a listing fall apart Tuesday. Inspection found foundation issues the seller didn't disclose. Buyer's lender killed it in hours. Thought we were done.

1. The agent didn't panic. Called me. We walked through three scenarios instead of one. That matters.

2. We pivoted to cash buyers before the listing went stale. Found two legitimate offers by Thursday. One closed.

3. The real win wasn't saving the deal. It was that the agent had someone to call who knew what to do when the obvious path disappeared.

Most agents sit alone with problems like this and watch deals die. They tell themselves it's the market or the buyer or bad luck.

When's the last time you had someone to actually call when a deal went sideways?

The gap between agents making 100k and agents making 500k isn't luck or market timing. It's three things.

1. They know their numbers. Not just revenue. Conversion rates. Cost per lead. Close ratios by source. They track it weekly. Most agents guess.

2. They protect their time like it's inventory. They don't take every call. They don't attend every meeting. They say no to things that don't move deals forward. The rest of us feel busy and call it productive.

3. They stay in their lane. They pick one lead source and own it completely before they add another. They get good at one thing instead of staying mediocre at ten things.

The agents at Lifestyle Design Realty who are hitting those numbers all three of these things in common. The broker's job is to make that possible. Not get in the way of it.

I've got agents at Lifestyle Design Realty who actually call me when things get hard instead of disappearing.

That didn't happen by accident. It happened because I stopped pretending that paychecks were the reason people stay. They stay because when a deal falls apart at 11pm, someone picks up the phone. They stay because when they're learning something new, there's a system and people to learn it from. They stay because closing a deal alone feels different than closing a deal knowing someone had your back the whole way. That's not soft stuff. That's the difference between an agent who stays two years and an agent who builds a career.

What would it feel like to work somewhere that invested in keeping you, not just recruiting you?

Agents leave for three reasons. Not one.

1. They're not getting real support when deals get messy. Your broker is unreachable or useless when things break. You solve it alone or you watch it die.

2. They feel invisible. The brokerage talks about culture but delivers isolation. You close deals and nobody knows. Nobody celebrates. Nobody helps you think through the hard ones.

3. They want to grow and there's no path. No mentorship. No systems to learn from. No one showing them how to scale beyond grinding leads every single day.

The split was never the issue. The issue was that you were running a solo business out of a brokerage office.

If you want to talk about what we're building at Lifestyle Design Realty, send me a DM.

Top earners track three numbers most agents ignore. Conversion rate. Cost per lead. Close ratio by source. They know these weekly. Not monthly. Not guesses. The second difference. They say no. To meetings. To calls. To anything that doesn't move a deal forward. Busy feels productive. It's not. Third. They own one lead source completely before adding another?

I spent two years telling agents that higher splits would make them happy. Paid out 80.20 splits. Watched them leave anyway. Then I stopped and asked the ones staying what actually kept them around.

It wasn't the commission. They said it was the same thing every time. I picked up when they called. We solved problems together. They didn't feel like they were running a solo business out of a brokerage office.

That's when it clicked. Most brokers have it backwards. They think agents leave for better splits. The real reason agents leave is because nobody's there.

I've talked to agents at big national brokers. They have lower splits than us. They have better technology. They still feel invisible.

The split doesn't matter if you're alone when a deal falls apart at 9pm.

Are you still convinced the commission structure at your current brokerage is actually what's keeping you there?
